item.title: From survey items to a scale, then on to regression and QCA: a step-by-step guide
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
NoteHow this article, the app, and the R script fit together

The step-by-step articles on this blog come with an app (a tool that runs in your browser) that lets you try the same procedure. The three have different roles:

  • The article explains the ideas and the procedure. The calculations are shown as R code.
  • The app (Scale Maker) reads your data (CSV) and shows the same calculations as the article on screen. You can learn the flow of the procedure and the meaning of the numbers without using R.
  • The R script: the app can produce an R script that reproduces the results of your settings on screen. You can run it in R and confirm that the numbers match the app. In research, you can also keep the script as a record of your analysis.

If you use R, start from the code in the article. If you learn with the app, read the article while looking at the numbers in the app first, and then reproduce them with the R script when you are comfortable.

The question this article answers

Research in marketing and management deals with concepts such as brand trust, perceived quality, customer satisfaction, and price sensitivity, which are hard to measure with a single question. These concepts are called constructs, and we measure them with several questionnaire items.

Suppose we measure brand trust with these three items:

  • Q1: This brand is sincere
  • Q2: I think this brand keeps its promises
  • Q3: I feel secure using this brand

What we want to know is not the effect of Q1, Q2, or Q3 separately. We want to know how brand trust, the three items taken together, relates to outcomes such as purchase intention. We also often want to use such constructs in later analyses: regression, logistic regression, QCA, cluster analysis, decision trees, and so on.

Structural equation modeling (SEM) is a wonderful method, but you do not have to start with it (and if you use it without understanding its characteristics, it can do more harm than good). What matters is not which method is more advanced, but how you measure the constructs of your research, and how you analyze them in the way that best fits your research question.

This article presents a procedure that works well for MBA research and empirical studies, with an example in R. The example data are generated with random numbers (they are not real survey data).

Scope of this article

  • We deal with constructs that you define in advance from theory and measure with several items. This does not deny the value of exploratory studies that look for constructs in the data.

  • We deal with measurement like brand trust, where we assume that one underlying construct drives the answers to several items in common. A person with high brand trust answers high on Q1, Q2, and Q3 alike. Therefore, the items are expected to correlate with one another (this kind of measurement is called reflective measurement).

    A different case is building a “customer behavior index” by combining purchase frequency, purchase amount, and years of use. A person who buys often does not necessarily spend a lot. The items need not correlate strongly, so the factor analysis and alpha procedure shown here does not apply as it is. It is not true that “for any index, you can raise alpha and take the average.”

The overall flow

  1. Define the construct from theory and prior research
  2. Prepare several questionnaire items for each construct
  3. Use exploratory factor analysis (EFA) to examine, in an exploratory way, whether the item groupings you expected are consistent with the data
  4. Align the direction of reverse-keyed items
  5. Check internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha)
  6. Build subscales by averaging items
  7. Use the subscales in regression and QCA

Let us go through them in order.

TipFor readers who learn with the app (this article)

“Example 3” in the app (Scale Maker) uses the same data as this article. Steps 2 to 7 in the app correspond to steps 3 to 6 in this article. Regression and QCA are done in R. The app’s calculation is the same as R’s standard promax. Depending on the version of psych, the third decimal place of the factor loadings can differ slightly.

Step 1: Define the construct from theory (before factor analysis)

This is the most important step. Before factor analysis, the researcher has to decide what to measure. Concepts such as “brand trust” and “perceived quality” are not things that statistical software finds for you automatically.

The approach to avoid looks like this:

“Let’s ask 20 questions for now, run a factor analysis, and name the factors that come out.”

This is a misunderstanding that beginners especially tend to fall into. The preferred order is as follows.

From prior research and theory, define what brand trust is, and think about the questionnaire items needed to observe it. When you prepared Q1 to Q3 above, you already held a theoretical expectation before the survey began: “these three items should be measuring one construct, brand trust.” You then run a factor analysis to check whether these three items actually move in the same direction in the real response data.

We do not build theory from factor analysis; we examine, in an exploratory way, whether the data are consistent with a measurement structure that we assumed from theory. This is why research on prior studies and theory beforehand is so important.

Factor analysis is not a machine that sorts items automatically

Suppose you run a factor analysis on 20 items and get four factors. That alone does not let you say that “human attitudes consist of four constructs.” What factor analysis shows is only the statistical fact that “in this sample, the correlation structure of this item set can be summarized fairly well by about four common factors.”

Whether those four factors are brand trust, quality evaluation, or brand attachment is not decided by the statistical result. You have to interpret them using prior research, the content of the items, the definition of the construct, and the purpose of the research. Please avoid giving plausible-sounding names to whatever factors come out.

Statistical grouping and theoretical validity are different things

Suppose four items, “high quality,” “good design,” “reasonably priced,” and “a well-known brand,” group into one factor statistically. That alone does not mean you may call the factor “brand value.” There are several possible reasons why items group statistically:

  • They really measure the same construct
  • Respondents tend to rate everything high
  • There is a halo effect
  • The item wordings are similar
  • There is a method effect from the same response format

A high factor loading does not prove that the items belong to the same concept in theory.

Step 2: Prepare several items for each construct

As a rule, prepare several items for each construct. Do not line up items that merely rephrase the same sentence. Items with the same meaning tend to raise Cronbach’s alpha, but this does not mean that the construct is covered adequately. It is desirable for the items to represent different aspects of the construct appropriately.

For example, compare these two ways of measuring brand trust.

An example of rephrasing

  • This brand is trustworthy
  • This brand is reliable
  • This brand is dependable

All three ask almost the same thing. The answers will be similar, so alpha will be high. But if you duplicate content to raise alpha, you can no longer tell whether the necessary aspects of brand trust are covered. Whether they are covered has to be examined separately. Note that when the concept you want to measure is narrow, items with close meanings can be appropriate, and they can also help average out errors caused by differences in wording.

An example of different aspects

  • I think this brand keeps its promises (the aspect of fulfilling promises)
  • This brand is sincere (the aspect of caring about the other party)
  • I feel secure using this brand (the aspect of reassurance in use)

All three are part of “brand trust,” but each looks at a different aspect, so the concept is captured more broadly. However, if you vary the aspects too much, the correlations among items fall and the items no longer form one factor. In light of the definition of the construct, choose items within the range where you can say they are “different aspects of the same concept.”

TipA questionnaire tip: labeling the options of a 7-point scale

There are two main ways to label the options.

  • Put a verbal label on all seven options: the meaning of each option is clear. On the other hand, words such as “very,” “extremely,” and “quite” feel different in strength to different people.
  • Label only the two ends and leave only numbers in between: this makes it easier to avoid differences in how strongly the words are felt.
Disagree  1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - 5 - 6 - 7  Agree

Which one to use depends on the purpose of the research and on the format of the existing scale you use. What deserves attention is that, in either form, treating the scores as equally spaced numbers is the analyst’s assumption (a simplification). The way of labeling does not guarantee equal spacing. In this article, we treat responses as numbers under this assumption.

If a scale has been used widely in prior research, using the existing scale is often better than writing items from scratch, because its validity has been examined and it is easy to compare with other studies. This does not mean, however, that “the existing study used three items, so we can use them as they are.” If the industry, culture, respondents, or purpose of the survey differ, the same factor structure may not be reproduced. Even with an existing scale, it is worth checking the structure in your own data.

Example data

From here we follow the steps in R. Suppose we measured nine items on a 7-point scale. The theoretical expectation is the following three constructs.

Construct Item Wording (example)
Brand trust Q1 This brand is sincere
Q2 I think this brand keeps its promises
Q3 I feel secure using this brand
Perceived quality Q4 This brand’s products are of high quality
Q5 This brand’s products perform well
Q6 (reverse-keyed) The quality of this brand’s products varies
Price sensitivity Q7 I notice even small price differences
Q8 I am tempted to buy when there is a discount
Q9 If products are similar, I choose the cheaper one

The wordings are examples (the data are generated with random numbers, and no actual survey corresponds to these wordings).

The outcome variable Y is purchase intention (one item on a 7-point scale).

Note

In this article, we treat 7-point responses as numbers and use Pearson correlation and linear regression. This is a common simplification in practice. If the response distributions are strongly skewed, you can also consider treating them as ordinal. For example, in factor analysis you can use polychoric correlations (fa(..., cor = "poly")). If purchase intention is measured with a single item, you can choose ordinal logistic regression instead of linear regression.

The following code creates the example data (the random seed is fixed, so you get the same data).

set.seed(2026)
n   <- 300
Phi <- matrix(c(1.0, 0.5, -0.2,
                0.5, 1.0, -0.1,
               -0.2,-0.1,  1.0), 3, 3, byrow = TRUE)   # correlations among the 3 constructs
Fm  <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n) %*% chol(Phi)
lam <- c(.80,.75,.70,  .78,.72,.68,  .75,.70,.65)       # item loadings (the "true" values)
fac <- rep(1:3, each = 3)
to7 <- function(z) as.integer(cut(z, c(-Inf,-1.6,-1.0,-0.4,0.4,1.0,1.6,Inf)))  # make 7-point responses
X <- sapply(1:9, function(j) to7(lam[j] * Fm[, fac[j]] + sqrt(1 - lam[j]^2) * rnorm(n)))
X[, 6] <- 8L - X[, 6]                                    # record Q6 as a reverse-keyed item
colnames(X) <- paste0("Q", 1:9)
b <- c(.45, .30, -.20)                       # effects of the 3 constructs on purchase intention
v <- drop(t(b) %*% Phi %*% b)                # variance of the signal part (including correlations among the constructs)
Y <- to7(drop(Fm %*% b) + sqrt(1 - v) * rnorm(n))   # add error so that the total variance is 1
dat <- data.frame(X, Y = Y)
head(dat)
  Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Q5 Q6 Q7 Q8 Q9 Y
1  5  5  3  3  3  3  4  4  6 6
2  2  4  2  3  3  5  5  4  5 3
3  4  4  3  3  4  5  5  6  3 4
4  5  4  4  4  5  1  5  4  4 3
5  4  4  4  4  2  7  3  4  4 4
6  2  1  1  2  2  6  4  5  5 1

Step 3: Examine how the items group, with exploratory factor analysis

Once the items are ready, examine how they group by using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). The role we expect of EFA here is not “to invent constructs from a state of knowing nothing.” It is to examine, in an exploratory way, whether the item structure we assumed from theory is consistent with the actual data. EFA is different from confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), which specifies in advance as a model which item measures which factor and tests it. The result of EFA is material for judging consistency with your expectation; it does not mean that the measurement structure has been verified.

First, as a guide to the number of factors, look at the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix and at parallel analysis. The count of eigenvalues of 1 or more is only a rough guide. Parallel analysis compares the eigenvalues of the real data with those obtained from random data, and uses the comparison as a clue to the number of factors. Decide the number of factors together with your theoretical expectation. Then extract three factors by principal axis factoring with promax rotation.

library(psych)
items <- paste0("Q", 1:9)
round(eigen(cor(dat[, items]))$values, 3)
[1] 2.918 1.921 1.107 0.640 0.584 0.528 0.490 0.462 0.350
set.seed(2026)
fa.parallel(dat[, items], fa = "fa", fm = "pa")   # parallel analysis (a figure appears)
Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors =  3  and the number of components =  NA 
fa3 <- fa(dat[, items], nfactors = 3, fm = "pa", rotate = "Promax",
          min.err = 1e-8, max.iter = 1000)   # strict convergence criteria for the iterations
Loading required namespace: GPArotation
print(fa3$loadings, cutoff = 0.3)

Loadings:
   PA1    PA3    PA2   
Q1         0.731       
Q2         0.724       
Q3         0.582       
Q4  0.769              
Q5  0.775              
Q6 -0.632              
Q7                0.695
Q8                0.674
Q9                0.639

                PA1   PA3   PA2
SS loadings    1.62 1.430 1.350
Proportion Var 0.18 0.159 0.150
Cumulative Var 0.18 0.339 0.489
round(fa3$Phi, 2)
     PA1   PA3   PA2
PA1 1.00  0.54  0.01
PA3 0.54  1.00 -0.20
PA2 0.01 -0.20  1.00
Note

To make the results easy to reproduce, this article uses rotate = "Promax" (with a capital P). The lowercase "promax" is not wrong, but its internal normalization differs, so the values change slightly.

min.err = 1e-8, max.iter = 1000 makes the iterations of principal axis factoring converge under strict criteria. The default criteria are loose, so the extraction can differ slightly around the third decimal place. To make the results match, this article uses the strict criteria.

Note also that the promax rotation calculation differs a little between versions of psych, and the third decimal place of the loadings can change (we confirmed a difference of at most 0.003 between psych 2.4.1 and 2.6.5). The extraction (principal axis factoring) gives the same result. The interpretation does not change.

Here is what to look at.

  • Number of factors: Look at the eigenvalues (the number of those at 1 or more) and the parallel analysis figure (the number of factors whose real-data eigenvalues exceed those from random data), and check whether they are consistent with the three factors we expected from theory.
  • Item groupings: Check whether Q1 to Q3, Q4 to Q6, and Q7 to Q9 load on the same factor, as expected. (Labels such as PA1 only indicate the order. Read the meaning of a factor from the items that load on it.)
  • The negative loading of Q6: Q6 has the opposite sign to Q4 and Q5 within the same factor. This is a clue that Q6 may be a reverse-keyed item. However, the sign is only a guide (the sign of a whole factor can be flipped). Whether an item is reverse-keyed is decided by the meaning of the wording.
  • Whether any item loads strongly on several factors (cross-loading).

For example, if only Q3 loaded strongly on the perceived quality factor, consider the following before deleting it:

  • Was the wording of Q3 appropriate?
  • Are brand trust and perceived quality conceptually too close?
  • Is there a problem with the translation or the phrasing?
  • Did respondents read it with a meaning different from the one we expected?

Use the result of EFA not as a “keep or delete verdict,” but as material for understanding the gap between the measurement model assumed from theory and the actual response behavior. If you mechanically delete a content-wise important item only because its loading is a little low, you may damage content validity.

Step 4: Align the direction of reverse-keyed items

Q6 is a reverse-keyed item. In practice, it is easier to follow if you decide the reverse-keyed items from the meaning of the wording before the analysis and align their direction in advance. In this article, we ran the EFA first, to show that a negative loading can be a clue. Use the minimum and maximum of the scale (here 1 and 7) and compute (minimum + maximum) − original value, that is, 8 - Q6. For 1 to 7, use 8 - Q6; for 1 to 5, use 6 - Q6. The same formula also works for a scale whose minimum is not 1 (for example, 0 to 10). Use the ends of the scale on the questionnaire (1 and 7 for a 7-point scale), not the minimum and maximum observed in the data. Whether an item is reverse-keyed is decided by the meaning of the wording (theory).

dat$Q6r <- 8 - dat$Q6

Step 5: Check internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha)

Once you have examined the factor structure, check the internal consistency of each item group. A typical index is Cronbach’s alpha. For example, indicates that the item group has relatively high internal consistency.

a_trust   <- alpha(dat[, c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3")],  check.keys = FALSE)
a_quality <- alpha(dat[, c("Q4", "Q5", "Q6r")], check.keys = FALSE)
a_price   <- alpha(dat[, c("Q7", "Q8", "Q9")],  check.keys = FALSE)
round(c(trust   = a_trust$total$raw_alpha,
        quality = a_quality$total$raw_alpha,
        price   = a_price$total$raw_alpha), 3)
  trust quality   price 
  0.731   0.774   0.705

There are two points to note.

  • A high alpha does not prove a one-factor structure. Alpha is an index of internal consistency, not an index for verifying factor structure. Also, alpha alone cannot tell you about reliability in general or about validity. The order is: examine the structure by factor analysis, then check the internal consistency of that item group.
  • Alpha tends to rise as the number of items grows. If needed, you may use McDonald’s omega alongside it.

Step 6: Build the subscales

Once you have examined the structure and checked the internal consistency, build a subscale for each construct. Usually the simple mean of the items is the default.

dat$Trust   <- rowMeans(dat[, c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3")])
dat$Quality <- rowMeans(dat[, c("Q4", "Q5", "Q6r")])
dat$Price   <- rowMeans(dat[, c("Q7", "Q8", "Q9")])
round(cor(dat[, c("Trust", "Quality", "Price")]), 2)
        Trust Quality Price
Trust    1.00    0.43 -0.14
Quality  0.43    1.00  0.01
Price   -0.14    0.01  1.00

A scale built from a simple mean still contains measurement error. An ordinary regression that uses such a scale does not model the measurement error explicitly. Therefore, the coefficients you obtain are not necessarily the same as the relationships among the latent constructs themselves. With low reliability, this effect can be larger. In multiple regression especially, the effect of measurement error also depends on the correlations among the predictors, so you cannot judge the effect on the coefficients from reliability alone.

A simple mean has the following advantages:

  • The calculation is clear and highly reproducible
  • It depends relatively little on the sample
  • The unit of the original response scale is kept, so it is easy to interpret
  • It can be used in both regression and QCA

Why not use factor scores?

Using factor scores is not wrong in itself. However, factor scores have problems: the weights depend on the sample, the values change with the estimation method, the meaning of the score itself is hard to grasp, and the scale may not be the same in another sample. Unless there is a special reason, a policy of using simple-mean scales whose reliability has been checked is quite reasonable for MBA-level research.

Where does confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) come in?

In exploratory MBA research, it is practical to build simple-mean scales based on the content of the items, the EFA results, and internal consistency. However, that alone does not mean that the validity of the measurement has been fully established.

How far to verify depends on the track record of verification of an existing scale, the extent of your changes, and the strength of the claim the research needs to make. When you want to verify the measurement structure explicitly, or when you have built a new scale or changed one substantially, consider additional verification such as CFA. In CFA, you specify in advance, as a model, which item measures which factor. If an existing measurement model is clear, you can also start with CFA without going through EFA. So there is no fixed order of “always do CFA after EFA.”

If your sample is large enough, a better approach is to split the sample, running EFA on one part for exploration and CFA on the other for verification. Even if you do run CFA, you do not necessarily have to use the CFA factor scores afterward.

Step 7: Use the subscales in regression and QCA

Regression

Once you have the subscales, you can run an ordinary regression.

summary(lm(Y ~ Trust + Quality + Price, data = dat))

Call:
lm(formula = Y ~ Trust + Quality + Price, data = dat)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-3.11817 -0.87767  0.06223  0.76259  2.85718 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  1.42862    0.37338   3.826 0.000159 ***
Trust        0.57160    0.06622   8.632 3.78e-16 ***
Quality      0.36507    0.05991   6.093 3.44e-09 ***
Price       -0.27133    0.05812  -4.668 4.61e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 1.157 on 296 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.4399,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4342 
F-statistic: 77.49 on 3 and 296 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

QCA

QCA needs a value of each condition for each case. In this example, the subscales of brand trust, perceived quality, and price sensitivity can be used as conditions. In fuzzy-set QCA (fsQCA), you calibrate each of them into set membership (values from 0 to 1). The outcome, purchase intention Y, is also calibrated into the set “high purchase intention.”

Then, for example, for the combination “high brand trust, high perceived quality, and low price sensitivity,” we examine a sufficiency relation such as the following (~ is negation and * is logical AND).

Points to note:

  • This expression is not an analysis result. It is an example of a combination to examine.
  • Decide the calibration anchors (full membership, full non-membership, and the crossover point) from the meaning of the set, not by mechanically converting the scale mean to a 0 to 1 range.
  • Y in the example measures purchase “intention.” Please write it separately from actual purchase “behavior.”

For the calibration and the analysis in practice, see the ThSQCA for beginners series.

What it means to use regression and QCA together

If you run regression and QCA on the same subscales, you can look at the same phenomenon from different viewpoints. Regression looks at the average association when the other variables are held constant. QCA looks at which combinations of conditions lead to the outcome. The two are better seen as complementary methods with different viewpoints than as competing methods. If you use common subscales, the measurement is unified across the two analyses.

What to report

In a paper or report, writing at least the following lets readers follow your procedure:

  • The definition of each construct and the source of the items (an existing scale, or one you created)
  • The sample size and how missing values were handled (for example, only complete cases were used)
  • The estimation method of the factor analysis (such as principal axis factoring), the rotation (promax), and the basis for the number of factors
  • The reverse-keyed items
  • The number of items and the alpha of each subscale
  • How the subscales were built (the simple mean of the items)

The whole procedure in a few words

A standard practical procedure has the following 11 stages. Steps 1 to 7 of this article rearrange these stages, except CFA (8) and SEM (11), in the order of building a scale (with a check of reverse-keyed items added).

  1. Define the construct from prior research
  2. Prepare several questionnaire items for each construct
  3. Hold in advance a theoretical expectation of “which item measures which construct”
  4. Use EFA to examine, in an exploratory way, whether that expectation is consistent with the actual data structure
  5. Examine the items from both theoretical and statistical viewpoints
  6. Check internal consistency with Cronbach’s alpha (and McDonald’s omega if needed)
  7. Build subscales by simple means
  8. Verify the measurement structure further with CFA, if needed
  9. Use the subscales in regression and similar analyses
  10. In QCA, calibrate the subscales and use them
  11. If the structure among latent variables is itself the research aim, consider SEM

The most important point is not “collect data and then look for meaning by factor analysis,” but “define the meaning from theory, and use factor analysis to examine, in an exploratory way, whether that meaning also holds in the data.”

You do not need to decide mechanically that “we use constructs, so we use SEM.” What matters is that the research question, the theory, the measurement, the way of building scales, and the method of analysis are consistent with one another.

This article does not cover why you might not use SEM, or how SEM compares. I plan to write about that in a separate article (Notes).

What to read next

The subscales you built in this article can also be used in QCA. While regression looks at the average association when the other variables are held constant, QCA looks for which combinations of conditions lead to the outcome. ThSQCA is an R package that shows how those combinations change when you move the target level (the threshold) of the outcome.

item.title: QCA in marketing and management: ten papers to read first (applications)
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
The basics list introduced the standard readings for learning QCA. The next question is probably “How is it actually used in research?” Here are papers from marketing and management that are worth reading as models for your own work, together with the theoretical background from management and organization research, grouped by purpose.

As in the basics list, the summaries stay within what the publishers’ abstracts say.

1. Applications in marketing and services

  • Ordanini, A., Parasuraman, A., & Rubera, G. (2014). When the recipe is more important than the ingredients: A qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of service innovation configurations. Journal of Service Research, 17(2), 134-149. https://doi.org/10.1177/1094670513513337 Studies luxury hotel services and uses QCA to examine which combinations of attributes lead to the adoption of a new service. An application that looks not only at individual attributes but at how they are combined.
  • Frambach, R. T., Fiss, P. C., & Ingenbleek, P. T. M. (2016). How important is customer orientation for firm performance? A fuzzy set analysis of orientations, strategies, and environments. Journal of Business Research, 69(4), 1428-1436. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2015.10.120 Combines customer orientation with other strategic orientations, strategy types, and market environments, and uses fsQCA to find the configurations that go with high firm performance. An application that considers the role of customer orientation through its combinations with other conditions.

2. Theoretical background in management and organization research

  • Fiss, P. C. (2007). A set-theoretic approach to organizational configurations. Academy of Management Review, 32(4), 1180-1198. https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2007.26586092 Treats an organization as a combination of elements and argues for analyzing the link between those combinations and outcomes with set theory. A foundation for thinking about several combinations that lead to the same outcome.
  • Fiss, P. C. (2011). Building better causal theories: A fuzzy set approach to typologies in organization research. Academy of Management Journal, 54(2), 393-420. https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2011.60263120 Analyzes organizational typologies with fuzzy sets and examines the combinations of conditions that lead to an outcome. Important for understanding that the causes can be asymmetric between the presence and the absence of an outcome.
  • Woodside, A. G. (2013). Moving beyond multiple regression analysis to algorithms: Calling for adoption of a paradigm shift from symmetric to asymmetric thinking in data analysis and crafting theory. Journal of Business Research, 66(4), 463-472. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2012.12.021 Alongside the effects of single variables in multiple regression, it proposes an analysis that looks at combinations of conditions and at causal asymmetry. It discusses how to analyze data and build theory, using regression and fsQCA on the same data.
  • Misangyi, V. F., Greckhamer, T., Furnari, S., Fiss, P. C., Crilly, D., & Aguilera, R. (2017). Embracing causal complexity: The emergence of a neo-configurational perspective. Journal of Management, 43(1), 255-282. https://doi.org/10.1177/0149206316679252 Reviews how QCA has developed in management and organization research and sets out a “neo-configurational perspective” for capturing causal complexity. It links set membership, necessity and sufficiency, and counterfactual analysis to theoretical viewpoints.

3. How to run and report an analysis (practical guides)

  • Greckhamer, T., Furnari, S., Fiss, P. C., & Aguilera, R. V. (2018). Studying configurations with qualitative comparative analysis: Best practices in strategy and organization research. Strategic Organization, 16(4), 482-495. https://doi.org/10.1177/1476127018786487 Sets out practical guidelines for QCA in strategy and organization research. It covers the whole course of a study, from model building and case selection to calibration, analysis, reporting, and interpretation.
  • Pappas, I. O., & Woodside, A. G. (2021). Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA): Guidelines for research practice in information systems and marketing. International Journal of Information Management, 58, Article 102310. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijinfomgt.2021.102310 A practical guide to using fsQCA in information systems and marketing research. It explains the procedure with data from earlier studies and also touches on checking predictive validity and combining fsQCA with methods such as SEM.
  • Park, Y., Fiss, P. C., & El Sawy, O. A. (2020). Theorizing the multiplicity of digital phenomena: The ecology of configurations, causal recipes, and guidelines for applying QCA. MIS Quarterly, 44(4), 1493-1520. https://doi.org/10.25300/MISQ/2020/13879 For digital phenomena that involve several theoretical perspectives and combinations of conditions, it offers a framework that ties QCA to theory building. Through examples, it explains how to apply QCA to deductive theory testing and to inductive theory building.

4. Choosing the threshold

  • Krogslund, C., Choi, D. D., & Poertner, M. (2015). Fuzzy sets on shaky ground: Parameter sensitivity and confirmation bias in fsQCA. Political Analysis, 23(1), 21-41. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpu016 Argues that fsQCA results can change with small changes in the parameters a user chooses, and that combinations containing randomly generated variables are often found to be sufficient for an outcome. It re-analyzes three existing studies and uses sensitivity analyses and Monte Carlo simulations.

On how the placement of the threshold changes the results, see also Toyoda (2026), Quality & Quantity, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11135-026-03092-3.

item.title: Papers and books for getting to know QCA: six to read first (basics)
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
The earlier posts explained why QCA suits decision-making and why the placement of the threshold matters. Here is a short list of the standard readings that people in any field tend to start with when they learn QCA, grouped by purpose.

The summaries below stay within what the publishers’ abstracts and descriptions say. They are not evaluations based on a full reading.

1. Getting the idea and the measures (papers)

  • Mahoney, J., & Goertz, G. (2006). A tale of two cultures: Contrasting quantitative and qualitative research. Political Analysis, 14(3), 227-249. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpj017 Contrasts quantitative and qualitative research as two cultures with different values, beliefs, and norms, and compares them across ten dimensions, including explanation, causation, case selection, and measurement. A starting point for seeing which research tradition QCA belongs to. Paper guide available
  • Ragin, C. C. (2006). Set relations in social research: Evaluating their consistency and coverage. Political Analysis, 14(3), 291-310. https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpj019 Introduces two measures for evaluating set relations, consistency and coverage. It shows that fuzzy sets overcome earlier limits on binary variables and on tolerance for error. Paper guide available
  • Schneider, C. Q., & Wagemann, C. (2010). Standards of good practice in qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) and fuzzy-sets. Comparative Sociology, 9(3), 397-418. https://doi.org/10.1163/156913210X12493538729793 Sets out standards of good practice for QCA and fuzzy sets. Useful for checking the procedures to follow before you start an analysis.

2. Learning the method systematically (books)

  • Ragin, C. C. (2008). Redesigning Social Inquiry: Fuzzy Sets and Beyond. University of Chicago Press. Contrasts set-theoretic analysis with conventional quantitative research and explains calibration, combinations of conditions, and causal complexity. A book for learning the way of thinking behind QCA, not only its procedure.
  • Schneider, C. Q., & Wagemann, C. (2012). Set-Theoretic Methods for the Social Sciences: A Guide to Qualitative Comparative Analysis. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139004244 A textbook that runs from the basics of set theory to the practice of QCA. It also covers cautions and common problems, which helps you understand the procedure together with the reasons behind each judgment.
  • Oana, I.-E., Schneider, C. Q., & Thomann, E. (2021). Qualitative Comparative Analysis Using R: A Beginner’s Guide. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781009006781 A beginner’s guide to running QCA in R. A good fit for readers who want to carry out the analysis in R and check the basic operations.

The next post introduces papers that use QCA in marketing and management, together with the theoretical background from management and organization research (applications).

item.title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 1: your first threshold sweep
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
This is the first part of a beginner’s series on ThSQCA, an R package for threshold-sweep qualitative comparative analysis (QCA). You do not need to know QCA beforehand. By the end of this post you will have run a threshold sweep yourself and read its result.

The one idea you need

QCA looks for combinations of conditions that are sufficient for an outcome. Suppose we study customer loyalty. A combination such as “high quality AND high service” is sufficient for high loyalty if (almost) every customer who has both also has high loyalty.

To do this, QCA first has to decide who counts as “high”. With survey scores from 0 to 10, we pick a threshold: a customer is “high” on a variable when the score is greater than or equal to the threshold. In this series, each score is split at the threshold into “high” and “not high” (crisp-set QCA).

Here is the catch. A threshold of 7 and a threshold of 8 are both reasonable, but they can lead to different answers. A normal QCA analysis picks one threshold and reports one answer. ThSQCA reruns the same analysis for a whole range of thresholds and puts all the answers in one table, so you can see where the answer holds and where it changes.

ThSQCA does not replace the QCA package. For every threshold, it calls QCA’s truthTable() and minimize() for you, with identical settings each time, and collects the results.

Step 1: install the packages

Run this once. (If you already installed them, skip it.)

install.packages(c("QCA", "ThSQCA"))

Then load ThSQCA in every new R session:

library(ThSQCA)

Step 2: create a small practice data set

To keep things reproducible, we simulate 400 customers. Each has four scores from 0 to 10: loyalty (LOY), and evaluations of quality (QUA), service (SER), and store environment (ENV). In this simulated world, loyalty is high when quality and service are both high, or (a little less strongly) when quality and environment are both high. A good analysis should discover this.

make_demo_data <- function(n = 400, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  QUA <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  SER <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  ENV <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  core <- pmax(pmin(QUA, SER), pmin(QUA, ENV) - 1)
  LOY  <- clip(core + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(LOY, QUA, SER, ENV)
}

demo <- make_demo_data()
head(demo)
  LOY QUA SER ENV
1   7   7   9   3
2   5   4   7   5
3   4   6   4   4
4   6   6   6   4
5   5   5   4   7
6   0   1   2   5

Each row is one customer. You do not have to understand the function above; it only produces the practice data. With your own data, you would simply read your file into a data frame with these kinds of columns.

Step 3: run the sweep

We want to know: how does the answer change as we raise the bar for “high loyalty”? So we keep the thresholds of the three conditions fixed at 7, and vary the outcome threshold from 5 to 8. This is called an outcome threshold sweep, and the function is otSweep().

res <- otSweep(
  dat         = demo,
  outcome     = "LOY",
  conditions  = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_range = 5:8,
  thrX        = c(QUA = 7, SER = 7, ENV = 7)
)

Here is what each line means.

Argument Meaning
dat the data frame to analyze
outcome the outcome column
conditions the condition columns
sweep_range the outcome thresholds to try: here 5, 6, 7, and 8
thrX the fixed threshold for each condition: “high” means 7 or more

Two settings are not written here because they have defaults: the minimum consistency for a combination to count as sufficient (incl.cut, default 0.8) and the minimum number of cases per combination (n.cut, default 1).

Step 4: read the result

summary(res)
OTS Summary
=========== 

Analysis Parameters:
  Outcome: LOY 
  Conditions: QUA, SER, ENV 
  Consistency cutoff: 0.8 
  Frequency cutoff: 1 

Results by Threshold:

 thrY        expression inclS  covS n_solutions
    5 QUA*SER + QUA*ENV 0.981 0.403           1
    6 QUA*SER + QUA*ENV 0.926 0.565           1
    7           QUA*SER 0.894 0.656           1
    8       No solution    NA    NA           0

The table has one row per outcome threshold. The columns are:

  • thrY: the outcome threshold used in that row. In the first row, “high loyalty” means LOY >= 5.
  • expression: the sufficient combination found. * means AND, + means OR, and ~ means NOT.
  • inclS: solution consistency. How reliably the cases covered by the solution are members of the outcome. Higher is better, and 1 is perfect.
  • covS: solution coverage. The share of the outcome cases that the solution explains.
  • n_solutions: how many minimal solutions were found (1 here).

Now read the expression column from top to bottom.

  • At LOY >= 5 and LOY >= 6, two combinations are sufficient: QUA*SER (high quality and high service) and QUA*ENV (high quality and a high store environment).
  • At LOY >= 7, only QUA*SER remains.
  • At LOY >= 8, the result is No solution. At this level, no combination of the three conditions reached the required consistency.

This is exactly what the simulation was built to contain, and it shows why a sweep is useful. Had we analyzed only LOY >= 6, we would have reported two paths. Had we analyzed only LOY >= 7, we would have reported one. The sweep shows that the answer depends on how high the target is, and where it stops working altogether.

A note on “No solution”: it is a technical result, not a statement that no route to high loyalty exists. It means that, for these data and these settings, QCA could not produce a minimal solution that meets the consistency requirement.

Step 5: see the result as a picture

A table is precise, but a picture shows the trend at a glance. The summary table is an ordinary data frame (res$summary), so we can plot it with base R. The next chunk draws solution coverage and solution consistency for each outcome threshold.

tab <- res$summary

plot(tab$thrY, tab$covS, type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 2, col = "#233A9A",
     xlim = c(4.8, 8.2), ylim = c(0, 1), xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Outcome threshold (thrY)", ylab = "Score",
     main = "Coverage and consistency by threshold")
axis(1, at = tab$thrY)
lines(tab$thrY, tab$inclS, type = "b", pch = 17, lwd = 2, col = "#F28018")
abline(v = 8, lty = 3, col = "grey60")
text(7.9, 0.3, "No solution\nat thrY = 8", adj = 1, col = "grey40")
legend("bottomleft", legend = c("Coverage (covS)", "Consistency (inclS)"),
       col = c("#233A9A", "#F28018"), pch = c(19, 17), lwd = 2, bty = "n")

As the target gets higher, coverage rises (the solution explains a larger share of the high-loyalty customers) while consistency slowly falls. At thrY = 8 the line simply stops, because there is no solution to plot.

What comes next

In the next part we will look more closely at the four kinds of sweeps (outcome, one condition, several conditions, and both together), and at how to choose the range of thresholds in a way you can defend.

The full package tutorial is available in the ThSQCA documentation, and the methodology is described in Toyoda (2026), Quality & Quantity.

item.title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 2: the four sweeps and how to choose a range
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
In part 1 we ran an outcome threshold sweep and read its result. ThSQCA has four sweep functions in total. This post runs all four on the same practice data, and ends with practical advice on choosing the range of thresholds.

The four sweeps at a glance

Question Function What varies What stays fixed
How does the solution change as the target level of the outcome rises? otSweep() the outcome threshold all condition thresholds
How sensitive is it to one condition’s definition of “high”? ctSweepS() one condition threshold the outcome and the other conditions
What if several conditions’ definitions change together? ctSweepM() several condition thresholds (a grid) the outcome threshold
What if the target level and the conditions’ definitions both change? dtSweep() the outcome and the conditions nothing

Setup: the same practice data as part 1

library(ThSQCA)
Practice data (identical to part 1) 
make_demo_data <- function(n = 400, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  QUA <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  SER <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  ENV <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  core <- pmax(pmin(QUA, SER), pmin(QUA, ENV) - 1)
  LOY  <- clip(core + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(LOY, QUA, SER, ENV)
}

demo <- make_demo_data()

Remember the story behind the data: loyalty (LOY) is high when quality (QUA) and service (SER) are both high, or, a little less strongly, when quality and the store environment (ENV) are both high.

Sweep 1: one condition with ctSweepS()

Suppose you are unsure where to draw the line for “high service delivery”. Is 6 high enough? 7? 9? Fix the outcome at LOY >= 7, fix the other conditions at 7, and sweep the threshold of SER from 5 to 9.

res_cts <- ctSweepS(
  dat          = demo,
  outcome      = "LOY",
  conditions   = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_var    = "SER",
  sweep_range  = 5:9,
  thrY         = 7,
  thrX_default = 7
)

summary(res_cts)

         7      QUA*SER 0.894 0.656           1
         8      QUA*SER 0.909 0.333           1
         9 QUA*SER*~ENV 0.917 0.122           1

The new arguments are sweep_var (the condition whose threshold is swept), thrY (the fixed outcome threshold), and thrX_default (the fixed threshold for all other conditions).

Reading the table from top to bottom: when “high service” is defined as 5 or 6, there is no solution, because the definition is so loose that the group of “highly served” customers is no longer reliably loyal. At 7 and 8 the solution is QUA*SER. At 9 the solution gains a third element, QUA*SER*~ENV, and coverage falls sharply, from 0.656 at 7 to 0.122 at 9. You can see why by counting how many customers are behind the strictest definition:

sum(demo$QUA >= 7 & demo$SER >= 9)                 # customers high on both quality and service
[1] 16
sum(demo$QUA >= 7 & demo$SER >= 9 & demo$ENV < 7)  # customers satisfying the solution QUA*SER*~ENV
[1] 12

Of the 400 customers, 16 are high on both quality and service, and only 12 of them also have a store-environment score below 7, which is what the solution QUA*SER*~ENV requires. The result there rests on very few cases. This is a useful habit: when a solution appears only at the edge of the grid, check how many cases are behind it.

Sweep 2: several conditions with ctSweepM()

Now let the thresholds of all three conditions vary at once: each of QUA, SER, and ENV is tried at 6, 7, and 8. That is 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 combinations. The outcome stays at LOY >= 7.

res_mcts <- ctSweepM(
  dat        = demo,
  outcome    = "LOY",
  conditions = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_list = list(QUA = 6:8, SER = 6:8, ENV = 6:8),
  thrY       = 7
)

The output has 27 rows. To keep it readable, show only the combinations that produced a solution:

Some patterns to look for:

  • Fourteen of the 27 combinations have a solution. In every combination where “high quality” is defined as 6, there is no solution at all.
  • With QUA at 7 and SER at 7 or 8, the solution is QUA*SER no matter which threshold is used for ENV. This is a stable region.
  • With QUA at 8, the solution depends on ENV (and on SER). With ENV at 6 it is QUA*SER (when SER is 7 or 8). With ENV at 7 it is QUA*SER*~ENV. With ENV at 8 it varies, from QUA*ENV alone to two-path solutions such as QUA*SER + QUA*ENV. When “high quality” is defined strictly, the definition of the store environment starts to matter.

The grid shows both where a conclusion is robust and where it is fragile, which a single analysis cannot.

Sweep 3: the outcome and the conditions together with dtSweep()

The dual threshold sweep combines the two ideas: it varies the target level of the outcome and the conditions’ definitions at the same time. Here we use 3 outcome thresholds (6, 7, 8) and 8 condition combinations (QUA, SER, ENV each at 6 or 7), so 24 cells.

A picture makes the same point faster. The next chunk draws the solution coverage of all 24 cells as a heat map. Each row is one definition of the three conditions, each column is one outcome threshold, and “none” marks a cell with no solution.
