How big is a sweep?

Every cell is a full QCA analysis, so the number of cells matters for run time and for how readable the results are.

Function Number of analyses Example
otSweep() one per outcome threshold 5 thresholds = 5
ctSweepS() one per threshold of the swept condition 5 thresholds = 5
ctSweepM() the product of the candidate counts 3 x 3 x 3 = 27
dtSweep() outcome thresholds x condition grid 3 x (3 x 3 x 3) = 81

Choosing a range you can defend

A sweep is easy to run, which is exactly why it needs discipline. Trying many thresholds and reporting only the convenient ones would add researcher degrees of freedom instead of removing them. Some rules of thumb:

  1. Decide the range before you look at the results. Base it on what the scale means, on theory, and on practical targets (for example “acceptable”, “good”, “very good”).
  2. Include your baseline. The threshold you would have used in an ordinary analysis should be inside the grid, so readers can compare.
  3. Avoid the neutral zone. On a 0 to 10 scale, scores around the midpoint do not clearly mean “high” for anyone, so ranges usually start above it.
  4. Keep the grid small enough to read. A few meaningful values per variable are better than every possible value.
  5. Check the case counts at the edges. Cells at the extremes of the grid often rest on very few cases.
  6. Report the whole grid. Show the stable and the unstable regions, not only the cells that support your story.

What comes next

In part 3 we look at the three solution types (complex, parsimonious, and intermediate) and at what to do when a cell has more than one minimal solution.

Software used: R 4.6.1, QCA 3.25.5, and ThSQCA 2.0.9.

item.title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 3: solution types and multiple solutions
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
In part 2 we ran all four sweeps. Two questions remain for a careful analysis. First, QCA can produce three kinds of solution (complex, parsimonious, and intermediate); which should you use? Second, what if a cell has more than one minimal solution? This post answers both with a second, smaller practice data set.

A second practice data set

We simulate 60 business software accounts. Each has a renewal score (RNW) and three evaluations: trust (TRU), price (PRC), and support (SUP), all from 0 to 10. In this simulated world, renewal is high when trust is high and either price or support is high. The three evaluations are strongly correlated, which will leave some combinations of conditions unobserved. That is deliberate, because unobserved combinations are exactly what the three solution types treat differently.

library(ThSQCA)
library(QCA)
Loading required package: admisc

To cite package QCA in publications, please use:
  Dusa, Adrian (2019) QCA with R. A Comprehensive Resource.
  Springer International Publishing.
Practice data set 2 
make_demo_data2 <- function(n = 60, seed = 89, rho = 0.85) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  L   <- rnorm(n)
  mk  <- function() clip(6 + 2 * (rho * L + sqrt(1 - rho^2) * rnorm(n)))
  TRU <- mk(); PRC <- mk(); SUP <- mk()
  RNW <- clip(pmin(TRU, pmax(PRC, SUP)) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(RNW, TRU, PRC, SUP)
}

demo2 <- make_demo_data2()
head(demo2)
  RNW TRU PRC SUP
1   3   3   4   4
2   6   8   7   7
3   9   9   9   7
4   5   5   4   6
5  10  10   8   9
6   1   2   4   5

Unobserved combinations (“logical remainders”)

With three conditions, each either high or low, there are 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 possible combinations. QCA lists them in a truth table. Let us build one by hand with the QCA package, using renewal of 5 or more as the outcome and 7 or more as “high” for each condition.

bin2 <- data.frame(
  RNW = as.integer(demo2$RNW >= 5),
  TRU = as.integer(demo2$TRU >= 7),
  PRC = as.integer(demo2$PRC >= 7),
  SUP = as.integer(demo2$SUP >= 7)
)

tt2 <- truthTable(bin2, outcome = "RNW", conditions = c("TRU", "PRC", "SUP"),
                  incl.cut = 0.8, n.cut = 1, show.cases = FALSE)
tt2

  OUT: output value
    n: number of cases in configuration
 incl: sufficiency inclusion score
  PRI: proportional reduction in inconsistency

    TRU PRC SUP   OUT    n   incl  PRI  
1    0   0   0     0     30  0.433 0.433
2    0   0   1     1     7   0.857 0.857
4    0   1   1     1     3   1.000 1.000
6    1   0   1     1     3   1.000 1.000
7    1   1   0     1     4   1.000 1.000
8    1   1   1     1     13  1.000 1.000

Look at the row numbers on the left. Only 6 of the 8 possible combinations appear (rows 3 and 5 are missing), because the data contain no accounts with, for example, high trust alone, or high price evaluation alone. The combinations that are missing are the logical remainders. The column n is the number of accounts in each combination, incl is how consistently they renew, and OUT is 1 when the combination is consistent enough to count as sufficient.

A bar chart of the counts makes the gaps easy to see. Each bar is one of the 8 possible combinations, in the same order as the truth table rows.

cells <- expand.grid(SUP = 0:1, PRC = 0:1, TRU = 0:1)[, c("TRU", "PRC", "SUP")]
cells$n <- mapply(function(a, b, c) sum(bin2$TRU == a & bin2$PRC == b & bin2$SUP == c),
                  cells$TRU, cells$PRC, cells$SUP)
cells$label <- paste0(ifelse(cells$TRU == 1, "TRU", "~TRU"), "*",
                      ifelse(cells$PRC == 1, "PRC", "~PRC"), "*",
                      ifelse(cells$SUP == 1, "SUP", "~SUP"))

op <- par(mar = c(4.5, 9, 3, 1))
n_rev <- rev(cells$n)
bp <- barplot(n_rev, horiz = TRUE, names.arg = rev(cells$label), las = 1,
              col = "#233A9A", xlim = c(0, max(cells$n) * 1.35),
              xlab = "Number of accounts",
              main = "Accounts per combination")
for (i in seq_along(n_rev)) {
  if (n_rev[i] == 0) {
    text(0, bp[i], "not observed (remainder)", pos = 4, col = "#B45309", cex = 0.9, font = 2)
  } else {
    text(n_rev[i], bp[i], n_rev[i], pos = 4, cex = 0.9)
  }
}
par(op)

The two combinations with no accounts are the remainders. Boolean minimization has no cases to check them against, so each solution type has to decide what to do with them.

Remainders matter because Boolean minimization can use them to make a formula shorter, and the three solution types differ in whether, and how, they do that.

Solution type Remainders used include dir.exp
Complex none "" (default) NULL
Parsimonious any remainder that shortens the formula "?" NULL
Intermediate only remainders that agree with your stated expectations "?" e.g. c(1, 1, 1)

Here dir.exp = c(1, 1, 1) says: we expect high trust, high price evaluation, and high support each to favor renewal.

The three solution types, side by side

We run the same outcome threshold sweep (renewal of 5, 6, 7, and 8) three times, changing only the solution type.

thr2  <- c(TRU = 7, PRC = 7, SUP = 7)
cond2 <- c("TRU", "PRC", "SUP")

run2 <- function(...) {
  otSweep(dat = demo2, outcome = "RNW", conditions = cond2, sweep_range = 5:8,
          thrX = thr2, incl.cut = 0.8, n.cut = 1, ...)
}

res_cx <- run2()                                     # complex
res_ps <- run2(include = "?")                        # parsimonious
Warning: Multiple equivalent solutions exist for thrY = 5 (n_solutions > 1).
Only the first solution (M1) and its fit metrics are shown. Use
generate_report() for full analysis.
res_im <- run2(include = "?", dir.exp = c(1, 1, 1))  # intermediate

data.frame(
  thrY         = 5:8,
  complex      = res_cx$summary$expression,
  parsimonious = res_ps$summary$expression,
  intermediate = res_im$summary$expression
)
  thrY            complex   parsimonious       intermediate
1    5      SUP + TRU*PRC      TRU + SUP      SUP + TRU*PRC
2    6 TRU*PRC + ~PRC*SUP TRU + ~PRC*SUP TRU*PRC + ~PRC*SUP
3    7            TRU*SUP        TRU*SUP            TRU*SUP
4    8        No solution    No solution        No solution

The warning shown with the output is a note from ThSQCA: at renewal of 5, the parsimonious analysis has more than one equally short solution. We come back to this below.

At renewal of 7, all three agree (TRU*SUP), and at 8 none finds a solution. At 5 and 6 the parsimonious solution is shorter. For example, at renewal of 5 it reports TRU + SUP, whereas the complex solution is SUP + TRU*PRC. The term TRU alone covers the combination “high trust, but low price and support evaluations”, which does not appear in the data. The parsimonious solution is willing to assume that this unobserved combination would also be sufficient. The complex solution makes no such assumption. In this particular data set the intermediate solution happens to coincide with the complex one.

How to choose:

Solution When it is a good choice Strength Caution
Complex Exploration; you want no assumptions about unobserved cases Every claim rests on observed cases Formulas can be long
Parsimonious You want to see the maximal simplification Shortest formulas May rely on implausible remainders
Intermediate Theory-driven reporting Uses only plausible remainders Needs a justified dir.exp

Whatever you choose, keep it the same across the whole sweep, and say which one you used.

When a cell has more than one minimal solution

Boolean minimization can return several equally short solutions for the same truth table. By default ThSQCA reports the first one (M1) and records the number of solutions in n_solutions. To see all of them, use extract_mode = "all".

res_all <- run2(include = "?", extract_mode = "all")
Warning: Multiple equivalent solutions exist for thrY = 5 (n_solutions > 1).
Only the first solution (M1) and its fit metrics are shown. Use
generate_report() for full analysis.
summary(res_all)
OTS Summary
=========== 

Analysis Parameters:
  Outcome: RNW 
  Conditions: TRU, PRC, SUP 
  Consistency cutoff: 0.8 
  Frequency cutoff: 1 

Results by Threshold:

 thrY                   expression inclS  covS n_solutions
    5 M1: TRU + SUP; M2: PRC + SUP 0.967 0.690           2
    6           M1: TRU + ~PRC*SUP 0.963 0.788           1
    7                  M1: TRU*SUP 0.875 0.667           1
    8                  No solution    NA    NA           0

Note: 1 threshold setting(s) had multiple solutions.
      Use generate_report() for full details.

At renewal of 5, the parsimonious analysis finds two minimal solutions of equal length (multiple minimal solutions), TRU + SUP and PRC + SUP. Each of them relies on a different unobserved combination, which is why neither can be preferred on the data alone. ThSQCA prints a note when this happens.

If you prefer a compact view, use extract_mode = "essential". It separates the terms that are present in every solution from the rest.

res_ess <- run2(include = "?", extract_mode = "essential")
Warning: Multiple equivalent solutions exist for thrY = 5 (n_solutions > 1).
Only the first solution (M1) and its fit metrics are shown. Use
generate_report() for full analysis.
res_ess$summary[, c("thrY", "expression", "selective_terms",
                    "unique_terms", "n_solutions")]
  thrY     expression selective_terms   unique_terms n_solutions
1    5            SUP       TRU + PRC M1:TRU; M2:PRC           2
2    6 TRU + ~PRC*SUP            <NA>           <NA>           1
3    7        TRU*SUP            <NA>           <NA>           1
4    8    No solution            <NA>           <NA>           0
Term type Meaning Here (renewal of 5)
Essential present in every solution SUP
Selective present in some solutions TRU and PRC
Unique present in only one solution TRU in M1, PRC in M2

ThSQCA records the alternatives, but deciding which one to prioritize is a theoretical judgment that stays with the researcher.

What comes next

In part 4, the last part, we turn the results into something you can report: a Markdown report, a configuration chart, and a check against the QCA package.

Software used: R 4.6.1, QCA 3.25.5, and ThSQCA 2.0.9.

item.title: ThSQCA for beginners, part 4: reporting and checking your results
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
In the first three parts we ran sweeps and learned to read them. In this last part we turn a sweep into something you can report and defend: a written record of what was explored, a chart of the configurations, and a check that the numbers agree with the QCA package.

library(ThSQCA)
library(QCA)
Loading required package: admisc

To cite package QCA in publications, please use:
  Dusa, Adrian (2019) QCA with R. A Comprehensive Resource.
  Springer International Publishing.
Practice data (identical to part 1) 
make_demo_data <- function(n = 400, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  clip <- function(x) pmin(10, pmax(0, round(x)))
  QUA <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  SER <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  ENV <- clip(rnorm(n, 6, 2))
  core <- pmax(pmin(QUA, SER), pmin(QUA, ENV) - 1)
  LOY  <- clip(core + rnorm(n, 0, 0.7))
  data.frame(LOY, QUA, SER, ENV)
}

demo <- make_demo_data()

We reuse the outcome threshold sweep from part 1. This time we ask for the full details, which the report needs.

res_ots <- otSweep(
  dat            = demo,
  outcome        = "LOY",
  conditions     = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
  sweep_range    = 5:8,
  thrX           = c(QUA = 7, SER = 7, ENV = 7),
  incl.cut       = 0.8,
  n.cut          = 1,
  return_details = TRUE
)

A report that records the whole sweep

A sweep produces many results, and a reader needs to know what range was explored, under which settings, and what came out at each threshold. generate_report() writes this into a Markdown file. It comes in two formats.

  • "simple" is a short report for the main text or an appendix. It has a summary table, the solution at each threshold, and code for checking the result with the QCA package.
  • "full" is for supplementary material. It adds an overview of the analysis (the sweep range and the cutoffs), descriptive statistics, and, for every threshold, the truth table, the solution fit, per-term metrics, a configuration chart, the QCA package output, and the settings needed to reproduce it. A comparison across thresholds follows.
report_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".md")
generate_report(res_ots, report_file, dat = demo, format = "simple")

Here are the first lines of the file it wrote. On your own computer, give the file a real name, such as "ots_report_simple.md", and it will appear in your working folder.

cat(head(readLines(report_file), 25), sep = "\n")
# QCA Analysis Report

*(Auto-generated by ThSQCA package)*

**Generated**: 2026-10-08 23:37

---

## Summary

| thrY | expression | inclS | covS | n_solutions |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | QUA\*SER + QUA\*ENV | 0.981 | 0.403 | 1 |
| 6 | QUA\*SER + QUA\*ENV | 0.926 | 0.565 | 1 |
| 7 | QUA\*SER | 0.894 | 0.656 | 1 |
| 8 | No solution | NA | NA | 0 |


---

## Solutions Overview

### LOY >= 5

**Solution**: QUA\*SER + QUA\*ENV -> LOY

A few options are worth knowing:

generate_report(res_ots, "r.md", dat = demo, format = "full")              # more detail
generate_report(res_ots, "r.md", dat = demo, include_chart = FALSE)        # no charts
generate_report(res_ots, "r.md", dat = demo, chart_symbol_set = "latex")   # LaTeX symbols
generate_report(res_ots, "r.md", dat = demo, include_raw_output = FALSE)   # omit QCA output

Configuration charts

QCA papers often show solutions as a chart: one column per path, one row per condition, a filled circle for “present”, a crossed circle for “absent”, and a blank where the path does not restrict the condition (neither presence nor absence is required). You can draw one from a list of paths with config_chart_from_paths().

paths <- c("A*B*~C", "A*D", "B*E")
cat(config_chart_from_paths(paths))
Condition T1 T2 T3
A ● ●
B ● ●
C ⊗
D ●
E ●

● = presence, ⊗ = absence, blank = don’t care

If you prefer plain characters, for example for a journal that cannot print the circle symbols, use the ASCII version:

cat(config_chart_from_paths(paths, symbol_set = "ascii"))
Condition T1 T2 T3
A O O
B O O
C X
D O
E O

O = presence, X = absence, blank = don’t care

How many cases stand behind each threshold?

A sweep table gives solutions and fit values, but not the number of cases behind them. A reader should be able to see that, because a result that rests on a handful of cases deserves less trust. For the outcome sweep of part 1, we can count the customers directly from the data, without ThSQCA.

thr <- 5:8
n_out  <- sapply(thr, function(t) sum(demo$LOY >= t))
n_both <- sapply(thr, function(t) sum(demo$LOY >= t & demo$QUA >= 7 & demo$SER >= 7))
cases <- rbind("High loyalty (LOY >= thrY)" = n_out,
               "... and high on QUA and SER" = n_both)
colnames(cases) <- thr

bp <- barplot(cases, beside = TRUE, col = c("#233A9A", "#F28018"),
              ylim = c(0, max(cases) * 1.15),
              xlab = "Outcome threshold (thrY)", ylab = "Number of customers",
              main = "Cases behind each threshold",
              legend.text = rownames(cases),
              args.legend = list(x = "topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.8))
text(bp, cases, labels = cases, pos = 3, cex = 0.8)

As the target rises, the high-loyalty group shrinks from 263 customers to 29, so the solutions at the strict end of a sweep are built on far fewer cases. Reporting these counts next to the sweep table is a simple way to show how much each row can bear.

Check a cell against the QCA package

ThSQCA does not invent new results. Every cell is an ordinary QCA analysis, so you can reproduce any cell by hand. This is a good way to build trust in the tool, and to answer a reviewer who asks. Here we reproduce the cell at an outcome threshold of 7.

bin <- function(x, t) as.integer(x >= t)

d7 <- data.frame(
  LOY = bin(demo$LOY, 7), QUA = bin(demo$QUA, 7),
  SER = bin(demo$SER, 7), ENV = bin(demo$ENV, 7)
)

tt  <- truthTable(d7, outcome = "LOY", conditions = c("QUA", "SER", "ENV"),
                  incl.cut = 0.8, n.cut = 1, show.cases = FALSE)
sol <- minimize(tt)
sol

M1: QUA*SER -> LOY

The solution printed by minimize() matches the row for thrY = 7 in the sweep table from part 1 (QUA*SER). In both cases the data were binarized in the same way (a score of 7 or above is a member), and in both cases the same QCA functions did the minimization.

Record your software versions

Results can depend on the versions of R and the packages. Print them and keep them with your report:

c(R      = R.version.string,
  QCA    = as.character(packageVersion("QCA")),
  ThSQCA = as.character(packageVersion("ThSQCA")))

A short checklist for reporting a sweep

Because a sweep gives you freedom to explore, it also asks you to be transparent. Before you report one, make sure that you can answer yes to each of these questions.

  1. Did I decide the threshold range, and the step between values, before looking at the results?
  2. Do I state every setting that was held fixed (consistency cutoff, frequency cutoff, solution type, directional expectations)?
  3. Did I report every cell of the grid, including the cells with no solution?
  4. Did I check how many cases stand behind the cells at the edges of the grid?
  5. If a cell had several minimal solutions, did I say so?
  6. Did I avoid presenting the sweep as a search for the best threshold?
  7. Did I record the versions of R, QCA, and ThSQCA?

Where to go from here

You now know the whole workflow: choose a sweep, set a defensible range, run it, read it, and report it. If you want more, the package documentation has the full tutorial with additional examples, and the methodology is explained in the paper.

  • ThSQCA documentation and tutorial
  • ThSQCA on CRAN
  • Toyoda, Y. (2026). Threshold-sweep QCA: threshold dependence as an analytical dimension. Quality & Quantity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11135-026-03092-3
  • Browser tools: QCA Quickstart and Sweep Builder

Software used: R 4.6.1, QCA 3.25.5, and ThSQCA 2.0.9.

item.title: Is “good enough” the same goal as “loved”? A marketer’s guide to threshold-sweep QCA
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
The previous post explained why QCA suits decision-making. One question was left open: where should the line between “high” and “low” go? This post takes it up.

Two managers in the same company are looking at the same customer survey.

The first wants to widen the base: get as many customers as possible to say the brand is acceptable to use. The second wants to build fans: create customers who really want to use the brand. Both ask the same question: “What combination of brand strengths gets customers there?”

Here is the uncomfortable part. A standard analysis answers that question for one cutoff. If you define “high” as a score of 7 or above, you get one answer. If you had chosen 8, you might have gotten a different one. Results across several cutoffs are not always reported systematically, so a single analysis cannot tell us whether the manager who wants fans and the manager who wants a wider base should be doing the same thing.

The cutoff is something to vary

Threshold-sweep QCA (ThSQCA) does not fix the cutoff in advance. It tries several. You run the same analysis at several cutoffs, with everything else held constant, and line the answers up in one table. You see where the answer holds steady, where it changes shape, and where it disappears.

If you have used top-box versus top-2-box scoring, you already know the problem. A result that looks solid at top-2-box can look very different at top-box. The sweep makes that comparison systematic.

A small example (simulated data)

To show the idea without using real customer data, we simulated 400 customers of a café brand. Each customer rated the brand from 0 to 10 on quality, service, and store environment, and also gave a loyalty score from 0 to 10. To keep things simple, we treat each rating as a yes/no split at 7 (crisp-set QCA). We then asked: which combinations of “high” ratings (7 or above) are enough for customers to reach each loyalty target?

Loyalty target Routes that get customers there How reliably Share of target customers explained
5 or above quality and service, or quality and store environment 0.98 40%
6 or above quality and service, or quality and store environment 0.93 57%
7 or above quality and service only 0.89 66%
8 or above no combination of the three is reliable enough n/a n/a

Read down the table as the bar rises.

  • A modest goal has options. There are two routes, so a manager can choose the cheaper one: improve quality and service, or improve quality and the store.
  • A demanding goal has fewer options. At 7 or above, only the quality and service route remains. The store environment stops being a way in.
  • A very demanding goal can outrun the data. At 8 or above, none of the three strengths, alone or in combination, was enough. That is not proof that no route exists; it tells you that these three strengths do not explain the very top. It is a cue to revisit additional conditions, measurement, the number of cases, and the analysis settings.

A single analysis at “7 or above” would have told the first manager something misleading: that quality and service is the only route, when for a broader goal there is a second one.

Questions where this helps

  • Satisfaction, recommendation intent (such as the NPS question), or purchase intent: does the recipe for “satisfied” equal the recipe for “delighted”?
  • Segment definitions: if “heavy user” means 10 purchases a year versus 20, do the drivers change?
  • Campaign targets: what does it take to move customers from “consider” to “prefer”?
  • Reporting: instead of defending one cutoff, show the range and let readers see how much depends on it.

Two honest cautions

  1. It shows combinations that go together with the outcome. It does not prove cause. This is true of any analysis of observational data. Treat the results as a map for where to look and what to test.
  2. Do not hunt for the cutoff that gives the nicest answer. Decide the range before you look, say why, and report all of it. The value of the sweep is in being transparent about how much the answer depends on the definition.

Try it on your own survey

You do not need to write code from scratch.

  1. QCA Quickstart creates a first analysis script from the names of your columns.
  2. Sweep Builder turns that setup into a threshold-sweep script.
  3. Paste the script into R. The package is free: install.packages("ThSQCA").

If you would like a gentler walk through the same ideas, the beginner’s series explains every line with a practice data set. The method itself is described in Toyoda (2026), Threshold-sweep QCA: threshold dependence as an analytical dimension, Quality & Quantity, and the package is on CRAN.

item.title: Why QCA suits decision-making: looking for “recipes” instead of single effects
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
A marketing manager’s question is not only “If we raise quality, will customers increase?” More often it is “Which things should we combine to reach our target?”

Qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) was built to answer that kind of question. Statistical methods such as regression are good at showing how much one factor matters on its own, with the other conditions held constant. QCA looks at the data from a different angle.

Why QCA is attractive for decisions

1. Actions are taken in combination, not alone

Store renovation, better service, and a price review are usually carried out together. QCA takes the combination (the recipe) as its unit, for example “high quality and high service”, and asks what happens to the outcome.

2. There may be more than one road to success

The same outcome can be reached in several ways (equifinality). Under the conditions and analysis settings you choose, QCA can identify several routes to the same outcome, so a manager can choose the one that fits the budget and the company’s strengths.

3. The reasons for success are not always the mirror image of the reasons for failure

The conditions that produce loyal customers and the conditions that produce customers who leave may need separate analyses (asymmetry). QCA analyzes the high case and the low case separately.

4. It can be used with small to medium numbers of cases

With stores, brands, campaigns, or corporate customers, you may have only dozens or a few hundred cases. QCA lets you analyze them while keeping an eye on what is inside each case, It can be used for small to medium comparative case sets. When there are few cases relative to the number of conditions, however, many logical remainders arise (combinations of conditions that no case shows).

5. The result reads as an “if … then” rule

A result comes out as a short rule, such as “high quality and high service”. It is easy to explain in a meeting, and it tells people on the front line what to do.

6. It separates “necessary” from “sufficient”

You can treat “without this, success does not happen” (a necessary condition) differently from “with this, success happens” (a sufficient condition). That lets you think separately about the actions you cannot skip and the actions that win.

How it differs from regression (roughly)

Point of view Regression QCA
The question How much does one factor matter on its own, with the others held constant? Which combinations are enough for the outcome?
Unit of analysis Each variable Combinations of conditions
Multiple roads Interactions and nonlinearity must be built into the model Can be identified as combinations
How results read Coefficients and significance Rules such as “A and B”
Typical scale Large samples Dozens to a few hundred cases

Neither is better than the other. You choose according to the question.

What QCA cannot do (and what is also true of other methods)

  • QCA is not the only method that cannot prove causation. Analyses of observational data, regression included, cannot fully establish causation. A sufficiency solution from QCA does not, by itself, guarantee the causal effect of carrying out an intervention. A causal reading needs support from research design, temporal order, theory, and case knowledge. The results are best used as material for thinking about candidate interventions and hypotheses to test.
  • It needs theory and knowledge of the cases. The analyst decides which conditions to include and where “high” begins.

The pitfall is the threshold

That last point matters more than it first appears. In QCA, the analyst decides the threshold that separates “high” from “low”. But a decision target is exactly such a threshold: do you aim for “reasonably satisfied” or for “loved”? When the threshold changes, the answer can change too.

Threshold-sweep QCA (ThSQCA) addresses this problem. The next post continues from here.

Next: Is “good enough” the same goal as “loved”?

References

  • Ragin, C. C. (2008). Redesigning Social Inquiry: Fuzzy Sets and Beyond. University of Chicago Press.
  • Fiss, P. C. (2011). Building better causal theories: A fuzzy set approach to typologies in organization research. Academy of Management Journal, 54(2), 393-420.
  • Woodside, A. G. (2013). Moving beyond multiple regression analysis to algorithms: Calling for adoption of a paradigm shift from symmetric to asymmetric thinking in data analysis and crafting theory. Journal of Business Research, 66(4), 463-472.

item.title: Introducing ThSQCA: threshold-sweep QCA in R
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
In qualitative comparative analysis (QCA), the thresholds that turn continuous scores into set memberships are usually fixed before the analysis. The resulting solution is then an answer to one specific definition, such as “usage intention is high” meaning a score of 7 or above. ThSQCA is an R package that makes the threshold itself an object of analysis: it repeats the same QCA analysis over a range of thresholds, under identical settings, and records how the sufficiency solution changes.

The idea

Changing a threshold changes which cases belong to a set. That can change the truth table, the fit measures, and the Boolean minimization. The relationship between a threshold t and the sufficiency solution S is therefore better described as a mapping, t → S(t), than as a single solution.

This is not the same question as a robustness check, which asks whether a favored solution survives alternative settings. It is also different from a search for the best threshold. Threshold-sweep QCA asks a descriptive question: how are sufficiency structures distributed across threshold definitions, and where do they persist, appear, or disappear? The methodology is developed in the paper below.

What the package does

ThSQCA does not implement its own minimization algorithm. Truth table construction and minimization are delegated to the QCA package, so the computational core is the same as in a standard analysis. ThSQCA adds the workflow around it:

  • the same consistency threshold, frequency threshold, solution type, and directional expectations are applied at every step of the sweep;
  • product terms, solution consistency, and coverage are collected into one common format;
  • cases with no solution or with multiple minimal solutions are recorded rather than lost;
  • results can be shown as tables and configuration charts, and written out as a Markdown report; the summary table can also be plotted with ordinary R graphics.

Four sweep functions

Question Function Threshold varied
How does the solution change as the target outcome level changes? otSweep() Outcome
How does it change as the criterion for one condition changes? ctSweepS() One condition
What happens when the criteria for several conditions change together? ctSweepM() Several conditions
How does it change when outcome and condition criteria change together? dtSweep() Outcome and conditions

Getting started

install.packages("ThSQCA")
library(ThSQCA)

The package includes a small example data set, sample_data, with an outcome Y and three conditions X1, X2, and X3, all scored from 0 to 10. The following is a minimal outcome-threshold sweep that runs as it is:

library(ThSQCA)

head(sample_data)

res <- otSweep(
  dat         = sample_data,
  outcome     = "Y",
  conditions  = c("X1", "X2", "X3"),
  sweep_range = 6:9,
  thrX        = c(X1 = 7, X2 = 7, X3 = 7)
)

summary(res)

This sweep asks how the sufficiency solution changes when “high outcome” is defined as Y >= 6, Y >= 7, Y >= 8, and Y >= 9. Each condition counts as “high” when its score is 7 or above. If you want a slower, step-by-step explanation of every row and of how to read the result table, see part 1 of the beginner’s series.

Running it prints a table like this (only the result part is shown):

 thrY                  expression inclS  covS n_solutions
    6 ~X1*X3 + ~X2*X3 + X1*X2*~X3 0.906 0.853           1
    7 ~X1*X3 + ~X2*X3 + X1*X2*~X3 0.906 0.879           1
    8                 No solution    NA    NA           0
    9                 No solution    NA    NA           0

Each row is one outcome threshold. In the expression column, * means AND, + means OR, and ~ means NOT. At Y >= 6 and Y >= 7, the same three sufficient paths appear. At Y >= 8 and Y >= 9, no solution meets the consistency requirement. A single-threshold analysis cannot show where an answer stops holding; a sweep can.

The package vignette covers all four functions with worked examples.

A note on use

ThSQCA is not a device for finding the threshold that gives the most appealing result. The range of thresholds should be justified in advance by the meaning of the scale, theory, and practical goals, and the range explored should be reported in full. The generate_report() function is designed to keep that record.

Links

  • Paper: Toyoda, Y. (2026). Threshold-sweep QCA: threshold dependence as an analytical dimension. Quality & Quantity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11135-026-03092-3
  • Package on CRAN: ThSQCA
  • Source code: GitHub
  • Documentation: im-research-yt.github.io/ThSQCA
  • Browser tools: QCA Quickstart and Sweep Builder

item.title: Welcome
item.dc:creator: Yuki Toyoda
item.description:
This blog collects notes on threshold-sweep QCA, the ThSQCA R package, and data analysis for marketing research.

Three browser tools are already available for generating R code: the QCA Quickstart for a first truthTable() and minimize() script, the Sweep Builder for turning a fixed-threshold QCA setup into ThSQCA sweep code, and the Scale Maker for building a scale from survey items step by step, together with the matching R script.

The articles are arranged in reading order on the home page. If you are new, start from the top. Technical posts with reproducible R code are in the beginner’s series for ThSQCA.
